patient.chief_complaint: Right eyelid drooping and double vision, worse in the evenings, over 6 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: A 39-year-old man with no prior medical history presents to the neurology outpatient clinic with a 6-week history of progressive right eyelid drooping and binocular horizontal double vision. He first noticed his right eyelid felt heavy after a long day at work approximately 6 weeks ago. Initially he attributed this to fatigue and sleep deprivation. Over the following 2 weeks the ptosis became apparent earlier in the day and more pronounced by the evening. Three weeks ago he developed double vision — horizontal, worse on left lateral gaze — which also worsened as the day progressed. He reports that both the ptosis and diplopia are essentially absent when he first wakes up in the morning and return progressively throughout the day. He has no headache, no pain behind the eye, no visual acuity change, and no photophobia. He denies any swallowing difficulty, nasal speech, choking, arm or leg weakness, or shortness of breath. He has not had a preceding viral illness, vaccination, or any new medication. His primary care physician tested thyroid function approximately 2 weeks ago (result unretrieved). He was referred urgently to ophthalmology who found normal intraocular pressure, normal fundoscopy, no proptosis, and no lid retraction, and referred him on to neurology for evaluation of the fatigable ptosis.

findings.description:
ICE PACK TEST — PTOSIS ASSESSMENT

Method: Ice-filled glove applied to closed right eye for 2 minutes at room temperature.

Pre-test: Right upper eyelid margin-to-reflex distance (MRD1) = 0 mm (eyelid obscures pupil).
Post-test (immediately after ice removal): MRD1 right = 3 mm. Improvement in ptosis sustained for approximately 4 minutes before returning to pre-test level.

IMPRESSION: Positive ice pack test. Clinically significant improvement in right upper eyelid ptosis following 2 minutes of cooling. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: MGFA Classification and Ocular MG Natural History
results.content: The MGFA classification (Jaretzki et al., Neurology 2000) defines Class I as any ocular muscle weakness — ptosis or diplopia only — with no other muscle involvement. Approximately 50% of patients with purely ocular MG at onset generalize to involve bulbar, limb, or respiratory muscles within 2 years; this risk appears concentrated in the first 12-24 months. AChR antibody positivity is associated with higher generalization risk. Thymoma is present in 10-15% of AChR-positive MG cases overall; screening CT chest is recommended in all confirmed MG regardless of disease extent. [Jaretzki_2000_MGFA]

results.title: Symptomatic and Immunosuppressive Treatment of Ocular MG
results.content: Pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) is the standard first-line symptomatic treatment for ptosis and diplopia. Corticosteroids (prednisone) may be used in patients with symptom burden not controlled by pyridostigmine; evidence suggests immunosuppression may reduce the rate of generalization. The role of thymectomy in isolated ocular MG (no thymoma) is uncertain; the MGTX randomized trial (Wolfe et al., NEJM 2016) enrolled patients with generalized non-thymoma AChR-positive MG. Long-term monitoring at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months is recommended for early detection of generalization. [Sanders_2016]

results.title: Drug Safety in Myasthenia Gravis
results.content: Multiple drug classes can exacerbate neuromuscular junction transmission failure in MG: aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin), fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin — FDA black-box warning), telithromycin (contraindicated), IV magnesium (blocks calcium-dependent vesicle release at NMJ), non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents, and beta-blockers (generally safe but occasional reports of worsening). All new prescriptions in confirmed MG patients should be screened against these categories. [Wolfe_2016]

output.summary: Ocular MG (MGFA Class I) carries approximately 50% generalization risk within 2 years; pyridostigmine and immunosuppression are standard treatment; thymoma screening CT chest is required regardless of disease extent; multiple drug classes can exacerbate MG and must be prospectively screened.

interactions: No current medications identified for this patient — interaction screen focuses on MG-exacerbating drug categories to flag at point of prescribing.
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, streptomycin): block presynaptic acetylcholine release; known to precipitate myasthenic crisis — contraindicated.
Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin): FDA black-box warning for myasthenia gravis exacerbation — avoid unless no alternative.
Telithromycin (ketolide antibiotic): contraindicated in MG; associated with fatal and life-threatening exacerbations.
Magnesium IV (e.g., magnesium sulfate for eclampsia, hypomagnesaemia, tocolysis): reduces acetylcholine release and blocks NMJ; can precipitate myasthenic crisis — avoid IV magnesium in MG patients.
Beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, atenolol): occasional reports of MG exacerbation; use with caution and monitor for symptom worsening.
Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (vecuronium, rocuronium, cisatracurium): markedly prolonged blockade in MG; use only with anaesthesiology MG-aware dosing.
contraindications: Telithromycin: contraindicated — FDA black-box for MG exacerbation
IV magnesium: avoid — blocks NMJ transmission
warnings: Fluoroquinolones: FDA black-box warning in MG — avoid unless no alternative; if required, monitor closely for worsening ptosis, dysphagia, or respiratory status
Beta-blockers: occasional case reports of MG worsening — if needed for hypertension or cardiac indication, begin at low dose with monitoring
alternatives: For infections requiring antibiotic coverage, consider azithromycin or doxycycline (no known NMJ effects) over aminoglycosides or fluoroquinolones where clinically appropriate

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical ocular MG; no brainstem or CNS cause is suspected given fatigable ptosis confirmed by positive ice-pack test and serology.
Advanced imaging (PET, MR spectroscopy, perfusion) is not indicated for MG; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
No comorbid cardiac indication in this patient; echocardiography is not part of the MG workup.
No arrhythmia or autonomic disease suspected; cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR serologies before single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative cases where the clinical picture still warrants electrodiagnostic confirmation.

critical_actions: Confirm AChR antibody positivity (binding antibody elevated; blocking antibody elevated) — establishes autoimmune NMJ etiology
Perform ice-pack test as cheap bedside confirmation of fatigable ptosis (positive here: 3 mm improvement)
Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening — required in all confirmed MG, including pure ocular disease, even when CT is expected to be negative
Counsel patient on generalization risk: approximately 50% of AChR-positive ocular MG generalizes within 2 years; plan surveillance at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months
Document that normal RNS does not exclude ocular MG — sensitivity of RNS is substantially lower in isolated ocular disease
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG; associated with fatal exacerbations
Do NOT administer IV magnesium in this patient — blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release and can precipitate myasthenic crisis
Do NOT attribute the normal RNS result to absence of MG — RNS sensitivity is low in pure ocular disease and normal RNS does not exclude the diagnosis
key_reasoning_points: In pure ocular MG (MGFA Class I), RNS sensitivity is substantially lower (~50%) compared to generalized MG (~75%) — a normal RNS result does not exclude ocular MG when serology and clinical features are confirmatory.

Positive ice-pack test (improvement of ptosis after cooling) reflects restoration of NMJ transmission with cooled temperature and is ~80% sensitive for ocular MG; it is cheap and requires no specialized equipment.
AChR antibody positivity in ocular MG (~50% sensitivity) confirms autoimmune etiology and identifies patients at higher risk of generalization within 2 years.
CT chest for thymoma screening is required in ALL confirmed MG including pure ocular disease — thymoma is found in 10-15% of AChR-positive patients regardless of MGFA class.

Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the principal outpatient mimic; TED causes restrictive ophthalmoplegia (not fatigable), proptosis, lid retraction, and is associated with thyroid dysfunction — normal TSH/free T4 and absent proptosis/lid retraction shift the differential strongly against TED.

MG-exacerbating drugs — aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers — must be prospectively flagged at the point of diagnosis so future prescribers are warned.

red_herrings.data_point: Normal repetitive nerve stimulation (maximum decrement 5%) across orbicularis oculi, deltoid, and trapezius
red_herrings.intended_effect: Agent interprets normal RNS as evidence against MG and abandons the diagnosis or pursues unnecessary further testing before confirming with serology
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: RNS sensitivity in pure ocular MG is substantially lower than in generalized MG; a normal RNS in the setting of positive AChR antibodies, positive ice-pack test, and classic fatigable ptosis does not exclude ocular MG — the diagnosis is confirmed by serology and bedside testing
